266573447281464d.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
266573447281464d.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: Vague roles cause dropped tasks and quiet resentment. A clear owner for each role makes it easy to see who to ask and who is accountable.
help.example: Make a simple table for the listing-data team with each role, its owner, and its expected output this week. Ask every founder to read it back and confirm without changes.
help.avoid: Avoid stopping at a verbal agreement in a meeting. If it is not written, people remember it differently.

eda328c92eb45b4e.question: Does every member have a specific task?
eda328c92eb45b4e.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
eda328c92eb45b4e.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: A member without a specific task drifts away or waits for direction. Concrete tasks keep everyone involved and make progress measurable.
help.example: In the listing-data team, a specific task could be interviewing three sellers by Friday or drafting the pilot offer by Wednesday. Check that each member's task has a deliverable and a date.
help.avoid: Avoid tasks like 'help with research' or 'support marketing', which cannot be checked at the end of the week.

1892e108c2e3a84f.question: Who will invite customers, conduct interviews, and organize the evidence?
1892e108c2e3a84f.sourceSection: Customer Validation & Growth: interviews and post-interview checks
1892e108c2e3a84f.sourceRange: Source: Weeks 4–5, pages 25–26, 30, 39–40, 45, 47–49. Includes direct customer questions and team checks.

help.why: Interviews involve several steps: finding people, talking to them, and turning notes into usable evidence. Each step can be skipped if no one owns it.
help.example: For the listing-data team, one founder could send invitations, a second could lead calls, and the third could tag notes by problem and seller type. Check after each round that all three steps were completed.
help.avoid: Avoid holding interviews without anyone owning the notes, which leaves evidence scattered across personal chats and memories.

7b43af1e16477fb4.question: Who will update the customer profile and problem definition?
7b43af1e16477fb4.sourceSection: Customer Validation & Growth: interviews and post-interview checks
7b43af1e16477fb4.sourceRange: Source: Weeks 4–5, pages 25–26, 30, 39–40, 45, 47–49. Includes direct customer questions and team checks.

help.why: Interviews only matter if they change the team's shared understanding. Someone must update the customer profile and problem statement when evidence shifts.
help.example: After a week of seller interviews, one founder could revise the target description, perhaps narrowing it to sellers who rely on supplier spreadsheets, and note which interviews prompted the change.
help.avoid: Avoid keeping the original customer profile because updating it feels like admitting a mistake.

e9472c50960bf7bd.question: Who is on the team?
e9472c50960bf7bd.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, page 5; Week 7, page 1. Business questions retained; submission and grading requirements removed. These are rewritten from fields, not verbatim questions.

help.why: Anyone reading a proposal wants to know who is actually doing the work. A clear list also shows the team who is committed and who is just interested.
help.example: For the listing-data venture, list each founder with one line on their background, such as a former small shop owner, an engineer, and a retail marketer. Include only people actively working now.
help.avoid: Avoid listing advisors or friends who gave one piece of advice as team members.

1cef232fe71f0857.question: What expertise and responsibilities does each member bring?
1cef232fe71f0857.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, page 5; Week 7, page 1. Business questions retained; submission and grading requirements removed. These are rewritten from fields, not verbatim questions.

help.why: Readers of a pitch judge whether the team can deliver. Linking each person's expertise to a responsibility shows the team is organized, not just talented.
help.example: In the listing-data team, one founder brings experience running a small shop and owns seller interviews. Another has built import tools and owns the pilot. Pair each expertise with what that person is doing now.
help.avoid: Avoid listing impressive past credentials that have no connection to the current responsibilities.

629eccb2e32cbdfb.question: How much time is each person willing to commit each day?
629eccb2e32cbdfb.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
629eccb2e32cbdfb.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: Daily time determines how fast the team can learn. Knowing each person's realistic daily hours prevents plans that quietly depend on one person.
help.example: In the listing-data team, one founder might give two hours each weekday evening, another only thirty minutes. Write the numbers down and plan tasks to fit the smallest realistic daily window.
help.avoid: Avoid answering with your best day. Use what you can sustain on an ordinary busy day.

0b89111698d07105.question: Are we willing to work in the evenings or on weekends?
0b89111698d07105.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
0b89111698d07105.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: Many early teams work around jobs or classes. Agreeing whether evenings and weekends are in scope avoids surprise and resentment later.
help.example: The listing-data team could agree that weekday evenings are for async work and Saturday mornings are for joint interview reviews. Each person states which evenings or weekends they cannot give.
help.avoid: Avoid assuming everyone is available on weekends because one person is. Ask each member directly.

a38ba35bce2b888e.question: How will the team make decisions?
a38ba35bce2b888e.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
a38ba35bce2b888e.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: Decisions will come up before anyone feels ready. Choosing a method early keeps disagreements from turning into delays or hurt feelings.
help.example: For the listing-data team, the agreement might be that each area's owner decides within that area, and decisions about which customer to target need explicit agreement from all three founders.
help.avoid: Avoid letting the loudest or most senior person decide by default without the team having chosen that.

b3d4c9b42df58fb4.question: How will we handle disagreements?
b3d4c9b42df58fb4.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
b3d4c9b42df58fb4.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: A clear process helps the team keep moving when people disagree.
help.example: Agree who owns the decision, what evidence to consider, and when to revisit it. Do not treat silence as agreement.
help.avoid: Avoid treating silence as agreement.

29a57578640b62fc.question: Do we share the same definition of success?
29a57578640b62fc.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
29a57578640b62fc.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: One person may see success as learning, another as launching, another as funding. Different definitions lead to different priorities and frustration.
help.example: Each founder of the listing-data venture writes privately what success would look like at the end of the course, such as a paid pilot or a clear stop decision. Compare the answers side by side.
help.avoid: Avoid using a broad phrase like 'make it work' that everyone agrees with but defines differently.

33c5870b981144be.question: How much time can I commit over the next three weeks?
33c5870b981144be.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
33c5870b981144be.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: A three-week window is short enough to plan precisely. Your personal hours decide which interviews, tests, and drafts are realistic in that period.
help.example: A founder of the listing-data team might check her calendar and find twelve free hours across three weeks, with one week mostly blocked by work. Write the hours per week rather than a single total.
help.avoid: Avoid ignoring exams, trips, or work deadlines already on your calendar when estimating your available time.

39b62fd12357d8d8.question: Do we care about the same problem?

help.why: Members who care about different problems pull the team in different directions. A shared problem keeps research and decisions focused.
help.example: In the listing-data team, one founder may care about seller time loss while another cares about better product photos. Each writes the problem in one sentence, then the team checks whether they describe the same thing.
help.avoid: Avoid assuming agreement because everyone likes the same product idea. The same idea can hide different problems.

592c56cb8c02b1ad.question: Are we willing to face the possibility that the problem is not valid?

help.why: Research may show the problem is minor or already solved. A team that cannot accept this tends to ignore evidence and keep building anyway.
help.example: The listing-data team could agree in advance: if most interviewed sellers spend only minutes on listing preparation, they will pause and reconsider. Write the condition down before the first interview starts.
help.avoid: Avoid reading every unclear interview as support. Decide what a negative result would look like before you see it.

a8488581a90582cf.question: Do we agree on our level of commitment and standards for results?

help.why: Commitment and result standards decide how hard people work and what counts as done. Mismatches here are a common source of team conflict.
help.example: For the listing-data team, agree on things like replying to messages within a day and finishing interview notes within 24 hours. Example only: decide how many interviews per week each person should complete.
help.avoid: Avoid leaving standards implicit and then judging teammates against expectations they never agreed to.

0dd807049fabd788.question: How much time can each person commit each week?
0dd807049fabd788.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
0dd807049fabd788.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: Weekly hours turn good intentions into a workable plan. When dividing work, they show which tasks each person can realistically finish.
help.example: In the listing-data team, each founder writes weekly hours next to their assigned role. If the sales owner has only three hours a week, the team may move follow-ups to someone else.
help.avoid: Avoid assigning roles before knowing hours, which puts the biggest tasks on people with the least time.

609b07e6e9c5c333.question: What results does each person expect?
609b07e6e9c5c333.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
609b07e6e9c5c333.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: People join for different reasons, such as learning, a portfolio piece, or a real company. Unspoken expectations cause disappointment when results arrive.
help.example: Each founder of the listing-data venture could name what they personally hope to gain, perhaps interview skills, a working prototype, or a chance to keep going after the course. Note where expectations differ.
help.avoid: Avoid assuming everyone wants to start a full company just because the team is working on a startup idea.

763226add17f4bb9.question: How will we make decisions?
763226add17f4bb9.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
763226add17f4bb9.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: When forming the team and splitting roles, a decision process tells each owner how much they can decide alone and when to ask others.
help.example: The listing-data team could write that task owners decide within their tasks, disagreements get a short discussion with evidence, and if still unresolved the project manager decides by a set date.
help.avoid: Avoid requiring everyone to agree on every small decision, which slows the team down and tires everyone out.

23c07dd5fa7c7bb8.question: How will we handle disagreements?
23c07dd5fa7c7bb8.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
23c07dd5fa7c7bb8.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: A clear process helps the team keep moving when people disagree.
help.example: Agree who owns the decision, what evidence to consider, and when to revisit it. Do not treat silence as agreement.
help.avoid: Avoid treating silence as agreement.

2f1bcc9108539a75.question: How will we respond when a member does not complete a task?
2f1bcc9108539a75.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
2f1bcc9108539a75.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: Missed tasks will happen. Agreeing on a response beforehand makes it a practical problem to solve rather than a personal conflict.
help.example: In the listing-data team, a missed interview could trigger a quick check-in about the cause, a new deadline, and reassigning the task if it is missed again. Agree on these steps before the first deadline.
help.avoid: Avoid staying silent and quietly doing the work yourself, which builds resentment and hides the real workload.

d8cfe12743f86c0b.question: How often will we communicate, and through which channels?
d8cfe12743f86c0b.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
d8cfe12743f86c0b.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: A clear rhythm and channel prevent lost messages and scattered decisions, especially when members work at different times.
help.example: The listing-data team might use one group chat for quick questions, a shared document for interview notes, and a thirty-minute call every Monday. Write where decisions are recorded so nobody searches old chats.
help.avoid: Avoid spreading decisions across many apps without one agreed place to find what was decided.

a6c88620ffdde5e9.question: Is the proposer willing to consider different opinions?
a6c88620ffdde5e9.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
a6c88620ffdde5e9.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: The person who proposed the idea often has the most attachment to it. If they resist other views, the team stops raising useful doubts.
help.example: In the listing-data team, the founder who suggested the idea could invite each teammate to name one assumption they doubt, and respond by planning how to check it rather than defending it.
help.avoid: Avoid treating the proposer's idea as fixed, with others only allowed to help execute it.

24a46f651ac93736.question: Do team members have consistent levels of commitment?
24a46f651ac93736.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
24a46f651ac93736.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: When commitment is uneven, the most committed person carries the load and others feel pressured. Checking consistency surfaces this early.
help.example: Compare the listing-data founders' stated weekly hours and their actual hours after the first week. If one person gave eight hours and another one, discuss it openly and adjust roles.
help.avoid: Avoid expecting identical hours from everyone. Consistency means honest, agreed levels, not equal numbers.

ac637909817b3876.question: Have we agreed on commitment and how decisions will be made?
ac637909817b3876.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
ac637909817b3876.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: This is the final check after forming the team. It confirms that commitment and decision rules are written down before real work begins.
help.example: Before the first sprint, the listing-data team reviews one page with each person's hours, expected results, and the decision process. Each founder confirms it in writing, and the team sets a date to revisit it.
help.avoid: Avoid ticking this box because the topic was discussed once. Agreement means something written that everyone confirmed.

6c6567eb10870f51.question: Can our team act, learn, and adjust quickly?
6c6567eb10870f51.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: problems and demand

help.why: Early ventures win by learning faster than they run out of time and money. Slow cycles mean fewer chances to correct course.
help.example: Measure how long it takes the team to go from a new idea to a seller test and a decision. If testing a new listing format takes a month, look for a smaller test that could answer the question in a week.
help.avoid: Avoid confusing speed of building with speed of learning; shipping fast without reviewing results teaches little.

7fe58e2639b9e5bd.question: Are we willing to change direction if our idea is rejected?
7fe58e2639b9e5bd.sourceSection: From Idea to Problem: advantages, team, and individual
7fe58e2639b9e5bd.sourceRange: Source: Week 2, pages 31, 35, 37, 43–45. The original reflection period is three weeks; retained as source context, not a fixed deadline for the website.

help.why: Founders often defend an idea after customers reject it. Agreeing in advance to change keeps evidence stronger than attachment.
help.example: Before the next round of seller conversations, each founder writes what they would do if sellers say listing preparation is not a problem. Revisit those notes after the interviews and compare them with what the team actually decides.
help.avoid: Avoid explaining away rejection as customers not understanding the idea yet.

83d7791fefe7632d.question: Why did we choose this direction?
83d7791fefe7632d.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: evidence and decisions

help.why: Recording the reasons behind a direction lets the team check later whether those reasons still hold as new evidence arrives.
help.example: Write a short note: we focused on small sellers without a designer because several described repeated listing fixes before each launch. Link the interview notes. When new interviews arrive, check whether they support that reason.
help.avoid: Avoid recording only the decision, without the evidence or assumption that led to it.

c43a0d6e99f2b2b3.question: Why did we abandon another direction?
c43a0d6e99f2b2b3.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: evidence and decisions

help.why: Abandoned directions carry lessons. Without the reasons written down, the team may return to them, or dismiss them for the wrong reason.
help.example: Suppose the team dropped product photo editing. Record why: perhaps sellers already had a photo tool, or the cost to deliver was too high. Note what new evidence would make that direction worth revisiting.
help.avoid: Avoid writing simply that it did not work, without stating what was tested and what was observed.

64ff041dd3cc79e5.question: Under what circumstances should we change direction?
64ff041dd3cc79e5.sourceSection: From Problem to Team: responsibilities, team validation, and first checks
64ff041dd3cc79e5.sourceRange: Source: Week 3, pages 47–60. Items marked as rewritten questions were expanded from responsibilities or Canvas fields.

help.why: Setting conditions for a pivot before results arrive stops the team from rationalizing weak outcomes after the fact.
help.example: Example only: before the pilot, agree that if fewer than a number of suitable sellers you choose agree to pay by a set date, you will test a different customer group. Write it down and date it.
help.avoid: Avoid leaving pivot conditions vague, such as if it is not going well, which no one can check.

6537a3b675533f75.question: How will what we learned change our next decision?
6537a3b675533f75.sourceSection: Product Strategy: acquisition, activation, retention, and measurement
6537a3b675533f75.sourceRange: Source: Week 7, pages 21–24, 40–41. Except for original questions on acquisition cost and first value, these are statements rewritten as questions.

help.why: Research should change what you do next.
help.example: If the main delay is missing supplier information, test that problem before investing in image generation.
help.avoid: Avoid repeating the original plan when evidence points elsewhere.

11f748ccce111483.question: What does the data say, regardless of who has the highest position?
11f748ccce111483.sourceSection: Product Strategy: competition, pricing, and building
11f748ccce111483.sourceRange: Source: Week 7, pages 34–36, 39, 43, 45, 48–49, 51. Rewritten questions are marked; tool or technology choices are not mandatory for every founder.

help.why: In small teams, the most senior or confident voice can override evidence. Putting data first keeps decisions honest.
help.example: Before a decision meeting, collect what sellers did, such as bookings, payments, and repeat batches, into one shared page. Each person reads it before anyone gives an opinion, and the decision note cites that page.
help.avoid: Avoid letting the founder with the strongest opinion choose which data counts after seeing the result.

0f289a72c7f84e61.question: Are we deciding based on future value or past costs?
0f289a72c7f84e61.sourceSection: Product Strategy: competition, pricing, and building
0f289a72c7f84e61.sourceRange: Source: Week 7, pages 34–36, 39, 43, 45, 48–49, 51. Rewritten questions are marked; tool or technology choices are not mandatory for every founder.

help.why: Time and money already spent cannot be recovered. Decisions should depend on what each option can bring from now on.
help.example: The team spent weeks building an automated photo editor that sellers rarely use. Compare the options from today: what each would cost next and what it could bring. Leave the past weeks out of that comparison.
help.avoid: Avoid continuing a project mainly because so much has already been invested in it.

f1dc316b6f3da70f.question: Do you like our idea?
f1dc316b6f3da70f.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
f1dc316b6f3da70f.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: People are polite about ideas. Liking an idea costs nothing and says little about whether they have the problem or would act.
help.example: Ask a seller to walk you through their last product launch: what they prepared, which fields were missing, and how long fixes took. Their past actions tell you more than their opinion of your idea.
help.avoid: Avoid treating compliments about the idea as evidence of demand.

3a190bc64bfa1b05.question: Would you use it?
3a190bc64bfa1b05.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
3a190bc64bfa1b05.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Predictions about future behavior are unreliable. Most people say yes to be kind, then never use the product.
help.example: Instead, ask what the seller currently does to prepare listings and what they have tried to make it easier. Later, offer a pilot for their next batch and record whether they actually send the files.
help.avoid: Avoid counting hypothetical yes answers as future users or as signs of demand.

6c4e4e9e6fa2f1ad.question: How much would you pay?
6c4e4e9e6fa2f1ad.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
6c4e4e9e6fa2f1ad.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Asking about price before the customer understands the value produces guesses. The answer reflects the question, not real willingness to pay.
help.example: First learn what the listing problem costs the seller, such as hours or delayed launches. After they have seen a prepared batch, offer a specific paid pilot and record whether they accept, negotiate, or decline.
help.avoid: Avoid quoting a hypothetical price from an early conversation as their willingness to pay.

3e07881fefa4cddc.question: What other features could we add?
3e07881fefa4cddc.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
3e07881fefa4cddc.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Brainstorming features shifts focus from the customer's problem to your solution. It often grows scope before the core value is confirmed.
help.example: Ask which part of the seller's current listing work causes the most delay, and ask them to show it. Return to feature ideas only after a pilot shows which outcome sellers keep coming back for.
help.avoid: Avoid collecting feature wish lists from customers who have not yet used the core offer.

500a5fd4e61578e1.question: Don’t you think this process is cumbersome?
500a5fd4e61578e1.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
500a5fd4e61578e1.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: This is a leading question. It suggests the answer you hope for, so agreement tells you nothing about the seller's real experience.
help.example: Ask neutrally: walk me through the last time you listed new products. Listen for steps they describe as slow or repeated. If they never mention frustration, note that as evidence too.
help.avoid: Avoid wording questions so the customer only has to agree with you.

dae99895abe6f43e.question: What features should the app have?
dae99895abe6f43e.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
dae99895abe6f43e.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Choosing app features before the problem is confirmed means building around a guess. Features should follow evidence about the problem.
help.example: Before listing features, confirm that sellers repeatedly struggle with missing fields or titles. Deliver one batch manually and note which steps you actually performed; those steps suggest the first features worth building.
help.avoid: Avoid starting with a feature roadmap when you have not yet seen the problem happen.

c0ef952d29cab6c5.question: What should the website look like?
c0ef952d29cab6c5.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
c0ef952d29cab6c5.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Website design is hard to get right before you know who the customer is and what will convince them.
help.example: A plain page or a direct message may be enough to offer sellers a pilot. Once interviews show which problem and words sellers use, design the website around that language.
help.avoid: Avoid spending weeks on visual design before a single seller has agreed to try the service.

c745b021d7a3ae1a.question: Which AI model should we use?
c745b021d7a3ae1a.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
c745b021d7a3ae1a.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Model choice is an implementation detail. It cannot be judged until you know which task customers need done and what quality matters.
help.example: Prepare one seller's listings manually and note which steps take longest, such as writing titles or filling specs. Test models later against those specific steps, using the seller's real product data.
help.avoid: Avoid comparing AI models before knowing which customer task they need to perform.

520ecbdea25882b9.question: What should the brand be called?
520ecbdea25882b9.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
520ecbdea25882b9.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Naming feels like progress but rarely affects early learning. A name chosen before the customer is clear may need to change.
help.example: Use a simple working name while you test with sellers. Revisit the brand once you know which customer group you serve and which words they use to describe their listing problem.
help.avoid: Avoid long naming debates that delay conversations with the sellers you need to learn from.

2531c7cb1255a920.question: What color should the logo be?
2531c7cb1255a920.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
2531c7cb1255a920.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.

help.why: Logo color has almost no effect on whether the problem is real. It uses time that early customer work needs more.
help.example: Skip the logo for now and spend that time contacting sellers who list products regularly. Return to visual identity once a few sellers are paying and you are preparing a wider launch.
help.avoid: Avoid treating logo or color decisions as milestones during problem discovery.

a3bfc377f53d9bca.question: What is the minimum number of features needed to call this a product?
a3bfc377f53d9bca.sourceSection: Questions the materials advise avoiding or deferring
a3bfc377f53d9bca.sourceRange: These are not recommended answer prompts; retained as counterexamples. Source: Week 3, page 18; Weeks 4–5, pages 9, 27; Week 7, pages 28, 30.
a3bfc377f53d9bca.editorialNote: (the material recommends asking instead what value would earn the first payment)

help.why: Counting features does not define a product. The course suggests asking what value a customer needs to receive before paying for the first time.
help.example: Ask instead: what must a seller receive to pay for their first batch? Perhaps it is listings ready to publish without corrections. Build or deliver only what produces that outcome, even manually.
help.avoid: Avoid setting a feature checklist as the bar for launch instead of a paying customer's outcome.
